sentences.text: Edestus was an extinct genus of eugeneodontid holocephalian fish, a group within the class Chondrichthyes, found in the Late Carboniferous of the United Kingdom, Russia, and the United States.
Its most distinctive feature was a tooth whorl consisting of numerous serrated teeth with long V-shaped roots stacked on top of each other like roof tiles.
Species within the genus are divided into two groups based on whether their tooth crowns are asymmetrical and slanting forward or symmetrical.

One species, E. triserratus, is distinguished by obtuse triangular crowns narrowing to a bullet-shaped apex, fine denticles, and a massive straight upper whorl base with a slender, tightly curved lower whorl.
A specimen described by Oliver Hay in 1912 as E. mirus preserved two whorls attached to jaw cartilage, definitively showing the whorls were situated in the mouth.
The largest species, E. heinrichi, was conservatively estimated to exceed 6.7 meters in length, potentially making it the largest marine predator known up to that point in history.
The largest known individuals of this species possessed an upper whorl 32 cm long and a lower whorl 43 cm long.

The genus was first described by Joseph Leidy in 1855, though the type species Edestus vorax has a holotype specimen that is very fragmentary, with its origin reported as Muskogee County, Oklahoma, though this location is disputed.

In 1855, Edward Hitchcock presented an Edestus specimen at a meeting of the American Association for the Advancement of Science in Providence; the specimen, a toothed frond, was originally found in Parke County, Indiana.
The specimen was lent to British anatomist Richard Owen in 1861, who referred it to Edestus and suggested it was a fin spine.
Edestus minor was described in 1866 by John Strong Newberry based on a single crown found in Posey County, Indiana, specifically specimen AMNH FF477, a single tooth crown lacking most of the root.
Edestus teeth grew at the back of the whorl, migrated forward through it, and were ejected from the front.
Tapanila and colleagues (2018) determined that the dental fronds functioned as effective tools for grasping and cutting soft-bodied prey.

The jaws of Edestus operated in a two-gear system involving the double articulation of the quadrate bone, allowing forward and backward jaw movements similar to streptostyly in modern lizards, with an output force of 1,907 newtons.
The parent group of Edestus is Edestidae, and the genus belongs to the family Edestidae.
Although 13 species of Edestus have been named, a 2019 analysis validated only four species spanning a six-million-year interval from 313 to 307 million years ago.
Classification in a separate genus is supported by the lack of a convex protuberance opposite the dental crowns, which appears in all other Edestus species.
Edestus lived during the Upper Carboniferous, from the Bashkiriense to the Moscoviense stages, with a time range from the Bashkirian to Gzhelian (323.4 to 298.9 million years ago).
These localities were situated in paleo-equatorial tropical latitudes.
Most Edestus remains are found in marine shales overlying coal swamp deposits due to marine transgression, though the genus is also known from estuarine habitats.
The earliest Edestus species appear in the late Bashkirian of the UK, with later appearances in Russia and the US during the Moscovian, coinciding with a rise in sea level.
E. triserratus lived from the upper Bashkirian to Moscovian in the US, UK, and Russia.

Due to the unusual nature of the dental fronds and the historical lack of cranial material, several hypotheses were proposed regarding how these structures functioned, with early hypotheses suggesting the fronds were either certainly teeth or defensive spines located on the fins.
It is debated whether the tooth whorls were attached to the dorsal fin, as proposed by Edwin Newton, or to the pectoral fins, as believed by Edward Drinker Cope.

Following detailed skull descriptions in 2004, researchers proposed two alternative feeding strategies: either an active predator ramming fish and using whorls like scissors, or a specialist jellyfish feeder.
Wayne M. Itano proposed that the fronds were arranged vertically to slice prey.
